statement: In a laboratory study of 6 men given methamphetamine by the smoked and the intravenous route on separate occasions, subjective and cardiovascular effects peaked within about 12 to 18 minutes and had largely subsided while plasma concentrations were still high, which the authors read as acute tolerance; no tolerance model was fitted, there was no placebo condition and the subjective scale was anchored to each man's own earlier experience (Cook et al., 1993). A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 men is consistent with the pattern: after intravenous dosing, cardiovascular and subjective effects peaked at 5 to 15 minutes and lasted up to about 6 hours, against a d-methamphetamine half-life of about 10 hours (Mendelson et al., 2006). Whether this reflects tolerance developing within a single dose, or effects that track the rate of rise rather than the concentration, has not been tested.
plain: After a smoked or injected dose, the effects people feel and the rise in heart rate come within about a quarter of an hour and then fade, while the drug is still in the blood at high levels. Researchers call this acute tolerance, but no study has tested it directly, and the main study here had six men, no dummy condition and no blinding.
population: Adults given single doses of methamphetamine in laboratory studies (6 men in one study, 12 men in the other)
exposure: Single smoked or intravenous methamphetamine dose (study conditions: a mean of 21.8 mg taken up from the device and 15.4–15.5 mg intravenous in one study; 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg intravenous in the other)
comparator: The same participants' plasma concentration–time course; placebo in the second study
outcome: Time course of subjective and cardiovascular effects relative to plasma concentration
magnitude: Peak subjective effect at about 18 min (SE 2.1) from the start of the smoked condition and 17.4 min (SE 1.1) after the intravenous dose; maximum heart-rate change at 11.8 min (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8), with effects subsiding while plasma concentrations remained high (Cook et al., 1993). Cardiovascular and subjective peaks at 5–15 min with effects lasting up to about 6 h, against a half-life of 10.2–10.7 h for d-methamphetamine (Mendelson et al., 2006).

evidence.extracted: Peak subjective effect came at about 18 min (SE 2.1) from the start of the smoked condition and 17.4 min (SE 1.1) after the intravenous dose, and the maximum heart-rate change at 11.8 min (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8); the figure plotting effect against concentration shows the effects subsiding while plasma concentrations were still high, and cardiovascular measures returned to baseline within a short period after both routes.

evidence.locator: Results, last paragraph of p. 719 continuing on p. 720 (left column)
evidence.extracted: Peak subjective 'high' reached 38% (SE 9.8) of each man's own maximum in the smoked and 41.5% (SE 20.1) in the intravenous condition; the smoked values are taken from the authors' earlier report on the same six volunteers, so they are not an independent measurement, and the scale is anchored to each man's own experience rather than to a common standard.

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Physiologic measures, paragraph beginning 'phetamine produced greater and longer-lasting cardiovascular effects'; Figure 4 (p. 413)
evidence.extracted: In a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover, cardiovascular effects peaked about 5 to 15 minutes after a 1-minute intravenous infusion and persisted up to 6 hours for conditions containing d-methamphetamine, returning to baseline within 2 to 4 hours after l-methamphetamine.
The half-life of intravenous d-methamphetamine in the same study was 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6), so effects had ended while well over half the drug remained in plasma.

risk_of_bias.note: The study the claim rests on had no placebo, no randomization of condition order and no blinding, and its subjective scale was anchored to each participant's own previous experience; the tolerance reading is an interpretation of two time courses, not a tested model.

imprecision.note: 6 participants in the primary study, no statistical test of the dissociation.

grade.reasoning: A laboratory administration study starts high (METHODS §6.3), but this one was open, unrandomized and without placebo, and the dissociation it reports was never tested statistically: −2 for risk of bias. Imprecision −1: six men. The supporting crossover (Mendelson et al., 2006) is placebo-controlled and double-blind but measured the time course, not tolerance, so it is recorded as consistent rather than as replication. The claim is worded as an observed dissociation between the time courses of effect and concentration, not as established tolerance.

changelog.change: New draft claim from Cook et al. (1993), read in full, with Mendelson et al. (2006) as a consistent observation. Section 5 of the monograph template has a slot for tolerance and no claim filled it. Anchors ai-located by the first reader and not yet checked.
